client: Hey Luna... I've been having a hard time since my dad passed away two months ago. Every time I visit my family now, it just hits me all over again how empty everything feels without him there. I'm not sure talking about it will help - it's not like it can bring him back.
therapist: It sounds like these family visits are bringing up a lot of pain and emotions for you. While your words express sadness, I notice a sense of urgency in how you're sharing this—almost like it's important to get it out quickly. What's it like for you when these feelings about your dad come up during those family gatherings?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It's like this heavy weight in my chest that makes it hard to breathe. I see his chair empty at the dinner table and I just want to run out of the room - but then I feel guilty for wanting to escape when my mom and siblings are right there grieving too. I don't know, maybe I shouldn't even be trying to avoid these feelings.
therapist: You're describing such a painful experience—this mix of grief and guilt that seems to overwhelm you in those family moments. I hear your voice getting higher and faster as you describe this, like the emotions are really pressing on you. Could we explore what thoughts come up when you feel guilty about wanting to leave?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I keep thinking "I should be stronger for them" and "If I leave, I'm abandoning them like dad did." But that last thought doesn't even make sense because he didn't choose to die... It's just this mess of emotions that makes me feel like a terrible daughter and sister.
therapist: I hear how tangled these thoughts and feelings are for you—this idea that you need to be strong mixed with the painful association between your grief and your dad's passing. Your voice sounds quieter now as you share this, like the weight of these thoughts is pressing down. Would it help to unpack that thought about "abandoning them like dad did" a bit more?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It's just...when I see how lost everyone looks without him, I feel like I have to stay and be the glue holding us together. But then I think about how he was always the one who did that, and now he's gone, so what if I'm not enough? That's when I panic and want to run. Talking about it makes my throat feel tight.
therapist: That tightness in your throat tells me how overwhelming this responsibility feels—like you're trying to fill shoes that no one could ever replace. You're carrying both your grief and this fear about whether you can hold everything together, which sounds absolutely exhausting. What do you think your dad would say if he could see you trying to take this all on yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: He'd probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself...he always said that. But it's different now. If I'm not hard on myself, who's going to make sure everyone's okay? I just feel like I don't have the right to fall apart when my family needs me.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding onto your dad's wisdom while also feeling the weight of this new responsibility. Your voice speeds up as you say this, like you're trying to solve this impossible equation of being strong while also grieving. What would it look like to be kind to yourself *and* be there for your family—are those truly opposites?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I never thought about it that way...but I guess when my sister cries on my shoulder, she's not expecting me to be perfect. She just wants me to *be* there. Maybe trying so hard to be strong is actually making me less present with them? This makes my chest ache in a different way.
therapist: That ache you're describing feels like an important realization—that being fully present with your family might mean allowing yourself to be human too. Your voice sounds softer now, like you're really letting this sink in. What would it feel like to give yourself permission to grieve alongside them, rather than trying to hold everything together?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It feels scary to even consider...like if I start crying, I might not stop. But maybe sharing our grief would bring us closer instead of me trying to be some kind of emotional rock. It's just hard to break that habit of holding everything in.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between this fear of letting go and this hopeful realization that sharing your grief could be healing for your whole family. Your voice carries a mix of apprehension and possibility as you say this—like you're standing at the edge of something important. What feels most vulnerable about the idea of letting your guard down with your family?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what scares me most is seeing my mom break down if I cry - she's always been the strong one, you know? Part of me worries that if we both let go at the same time, we'll just drown in it. But another part wonders if she's thinking the same thing about me.
therapist: You're describing this beautiful but painful mirror between you and your mom—both wanting to protect each other while grieving yourselves. I hear your voice getting higher and faster as you talk about this, like you're trying to outrun the emotions even while putting words to them. What would it be like to test this fear—maybe start with sharing just a little of your grief with her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know...what if I try to share something small and she just shuts down? Or worse, what if she starts crying and I can't handle it? I feel like I barely have a grip on my own emotions, let alone being able to comfort her. Maybe we're better off just keeping things surface-level for now.
therapist: You're carrying so much worry about how your mom might react—this fear that neither of you can handle the other's grief right now. I hear how carefully you're considering this, with your voice staying steady even as you talk about these difficult possibilities. What makes you think that keeping things surface-level is truly protecting either of you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I tell myself it's protection because at least we're not making each other feel worse. But when I really think about it...we're both just sitting alone with our pain. It's just easier to pretend we're okay than to risk making things harder. But now that I say that out loud, it sounds so lonely.
therapist: You've put words to something so important—this realization that what feels like protection might actually be keeping you both isolated in your grief. Your voice sounds softer and more reflective as you share this, like you're really letting this truth sink in. How does it feel to acknowledge that perhaps you and your mom might be ready to share your grief rather than protecting each other from it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
